per_quote.text: The goal of the present research was to examine how political climate moderates the relationship between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.

Controlling for age, education, income, and race, there was an interaction between political conservatism and conservative political climate for both vaccine and booster hesitancy... such that liberals were less likely to be hesitant regardless of political climate. However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.

The interaction for self-reported booster status was consistent with those for vaccine and booster hesitancy... as political conservatism increased, the likelihood of receiving a booster was lower for participants in a conservative regional climate as compared to those in a liberal regional climate.

We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023... We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times... We used this % Republican vote by zip code as a measure of conservative regional climate.

Self-reported vaccine status and booster status were assessed through individual items... Vaccine hesitancy... was measured using the seven items from the Attitudes towards Adult Vaccination Scale... Booster hesitancy was assessed using items from a 2022 survey on COVID-19 booster hesitancy.

Political conservatism and conservative regional climate were positively associated with vaccine hesitancy (β = .23, p < .001; β = .11, p = .001; respectively)... Additionally, the interaction between political conservatism and conservative regional climate was significant (β = .09, p = .003).

Political conservatism and conservative regional climate were negatively associated with booster status (OR =.82, p = .022; OR =.77, p = .004; respectively). Additionally, there was a significant interaction... between political conservatism and conservative regional climate (OR =.83, p = .026).

The most strikingly, for booster status the interaction between political orientation and political climate indicated that the most liberal participants were over 65% likely to get boosted regardless of climate.
There was no difference in the likelihood of reporting receiving a booster based on conservative regional climate for the most politically liberal participants...
Conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.
The most conservative participants in liberal climates were 60% likely to get boosted, while conservatives in conservative climates were less than 35% likely to get boosted.
The interaction between political conservatism and conservative regional climate (Table 6) was not significant (OR = 1.02, p = .833) [for vaccine status].
The interaction for vaccination was not significant, this difference between attitudes (hesitancy) and action (vaccination), likely reflects the high prevalence of COVID-19 vaccine mandates.
Finally, it should be noted that this data is cross-sectional and we cannot assume causal or directional associations.

Because we used 2020 presidential election votes by zip code as a proxy for political climate, it must be noted that other zip code-based differences could be driving the associations noted in this paper. Regional factors (e.g., population density) may play a role...

Additionally, our sample was recruited through an online platform and only includes participants with access to this platform. Further, our sample includes only White and Black participants recruited through Qualtrics Panels, and may not generalize to broader populations in the United States.

Another limitation in this dataset is the reliance on self-reported vaccine status. Self-report is susceptible to social desirability [30] and recall bias [31], and we cannot assume that reported vaccine status reflects actual vaccine status.

While previous research has identified the unique impact of both political orientation and political climate on vaccination attitudes, there has been little research on the interaction between personal political orientation and local political climate.

By looking at political orientation and region climate, we identify a novel and important finding, specifically that conservative individuals are more likely to received booster doses in liberal regions.

The influence of political orientation on vaccine hesitancy has been increasing since the onset of the pandemic and political orientation has become a better predictor of vaccine hesitancy than demographic variables, pandemic-related fear, and trust in health institutions [18].
These findings suggest that environmental factors (e.g., social pressure) may impact decisions to receive annual COVID-19 doses.
This study introduces a novel computational approach to measure subnational and event-driven variation in partisan polarization and explores these dynamics across the United States and Canada.

Our analysis reveals that politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States.

We demonstrate a strong negative correlation between regional vaccination rates and the degree of polarization in vaccine-related discussions in the U.S., suggesting tangible public health implications of online partisan division.
This relationship was notably weaker in Canada, pointing to important cross-national differences in how political polarization manifests and impacts health behaviors.

Analyzing over 50 million tweets from late 2020—a critical period of polarizing discourse during the pandemic’s early phase—we examine regional variations in discussions surrounding three key health interventions: lockdowns, masks, and vaccines.

We collected a large-scale dataset of COVID-19 political discussions on Twitter (now X) occurring between October 9, 2020, to January 4, 2021, comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada.
We verified that our data provided a politically balanced representation of users across different regions in both countries by comparing with official population census data and election results.

In the United States (Fig 9), conservative states consistently show higher polarization overall and specifically in discussions related to masks and vaccines. The lockdown discourse shows a more mixed pattern... However, the general relationship between state partisanship and polarization remains evident
In Canada (Fig 9), Alberta, a conservative province, exhibits higher polarization compared to Ontario and British Columbia

Importantly, we observe that vaccine polarization is strongly negatively correlated with actual vaccination rates across American states (Fig 12)... Using official CDC vaccination data... we confirm a strong negative correlation (r = −0.77, p < 0.001) between vaccine polarization and vaccination rates.

By tracking the temporal evolution of polarization, we identify distinct spikes linked to specific political events and policy announcements. These polarization surges typically lasted only a few days, revealing the dynamic nature of online partisan discourse.
The profiles by partisan affiliation (Fig 15A,C) show that conservative partisans in both countries tweet conspiracy-related content at higher rates than progressive partisans.

When correlated with aggregate daily polarization (Fig 15 B and D, we find a small but significant negative correlation for the United States, while no significant correlation was observed for Canada.

Quebec ranks highest overall, though we acknowledge a limitation of our English-focused analysis in this predominantly French-speaking province, which experienced significant pandemic-related polarization including violent protests
Our results confirmed that Quebec had the highest level of partisan division over vaccines, alongside the highest reported COVID-19 incidence in Canada during the first and second pandemic waves

While we cannot establish causality among conservative voting patterns, polarization scores, and vaccination rates, our results suggest polarized discourse played a significant role in shaping the heterogeneous vaccination landscape across the U.S.

While our polarization index reflects the discourse of politically engaged Twitter users, it nevertheless captures key dynamics of online debate that influence public narratives and align with observable regional outcomes.
Finally, while several of our analyses rely on correlations, these results do not imply causation.

Third, our analysis is based on Twitter (X) data, which may not fully capture the views and sentiments of the broader American and Canadian public... Fourth, we restricted our analysis to English-language tweets, which in Canada means we primarily captured perspectives of either anglophones or bilingual francophones — a potential source of bias.

Recent computational approaches increasingly draw on text embedding methods to study polarization... However, access to user- and network-level data has become increasingly restricted... Consequently, our study adopts a strictly text-based method, which remains both accessible and scalable for analyzing large-scale digital discourse.

In line with previous research ((e.g., [17,58–60])), we found that more right leaning states and provinces exhibited greater partisan divisions around COVID-19 on Twitter (X)... However, we extended beyond these studies to characterize the geographic heterogeneity and temporal evolution of polarization, connecting features in our polarization metric to real-world events.

To test for the possibility of stigmatizing language spillover, this preliminary study employs a survey experiment testing exposure to the Party’s advertisement, labeling Trump as a “convicted criminal” (n = 814) relative to no advertisement (n = 813), on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with records and several dimensions of perceived representation.

Thus, this study explores what may have been the impact of propagating such labels on Democrats’ perceptions of people with criminal records, and to what extent does the propagation of such stigmatizing terminology impact how well Democrats perceive to be represented by their own elected officials?

Results suggest that exposure to the Trump advertisement with the “convicted criminal” label had significant, negative impacts on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with records, but improved perceived feelings of representation. Importantly, the effect of a counter-stereotype’s ability to mitigate these effects was also tested... Findings suggest that the counter-stereotype vastly ameliorated the negative effects of the advertisement on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with criminal records.

First, there is clear evidence that the Trump advertisement caused decreases in positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records amongst Democrats, but when paired with (and preceded by) a counter-narrative of a dedicated, system-impacted state representative who speaks to the harm of the “criminal” label, these effects were almost entirely ameliorated

Thus, the 2,439 participants were allocated approximately evenly across one of three different treatment groups: a) the Control group (n = 813); b) the Trump Ad Alone group (n = 814); and c) the Counter-Narrative First group (n = 812).

The survey was fielded through Prolific, an online survey platform that is commonly utilized for conducting survey-based research... 2,500 participants were recruited for this study, between July 12th and 13th of 2025... the study sample focused only on their constituents.

Hypothesis 2A: Being presented with the Democratic party’s Trump advertisement alone, labeling him as a “convicted criminal,” will significantly decrease (positive) perceptions of individuals with criminal records, on average, relative to not being exposed to this advertisement
Both H2A and H2B were supported, namely, exposure to the Trump advertisement alone significantly decreased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records ( β̂0 = −0.835, SE = 0.044)

The most profound impact of the counternarrative, unsurprisingly, given the content of the counter-narrative, was on the perceptions of individuals with criminal records (H1B): exposure to the counter-narrative prior to being presented with the Trump advertisement increased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records by more than 0.8 standard deviation (SD) units, compared to those presented with the Trump advertisement alone

Additionally, exposure to the Trump advertisement significantly increased feelings of being well represented by elected officials and the extent to which Democrats perceived that elected officials were motivated by public service over self-interest.
Starting with H1A, exposure to the counter-narrative significantly decreased support for the Trump advertisement, relative to the Trump advertisement alone ( β̂2 = −0.172 SE = 0.048).

Additionally, evidence supported H1D, namely that exposure to the counter-narrative significantly decreased quality of Democratic representation in federal government, relative to just Trump advertisement exposure ( β̂2 = −0.332, SE = 0.048).

Specifically, for the items about possession of having a criminal record being a reflection of someone’s character, that most people with criminal records do not positively contribute to their communities (which was reverse-coded), and that labeling people with records as ‘criminals’ may do more harm than good, the Trump advertisement exposure appeared to be significantly more damaging to perceptions of individuals with criminal records for those who are system-impacted.

First, the ideal version of this survey experiment would have been to utilize a full factorial design... failing to include the counter-narrative only arm limits the ability to interpret the additional impact of including it with the advertisements

It is also incredibly important to acknowledge that this survey was fielded amongst an online panel of survey respondents, and the proliferation of generative AI should cause concerns over the humanity of the responses provided within the survey.

as the advertisement (i.e., Trump’s mugshot with the words ‘convicted criminal’ imposed on the image) was presented consistently across treatment arms, it is not possible to disentangle the impact of the image from the stigmatizing terminology imposed
Leaning upon social categorization theory, propagating such labels on Trump may thereby spillover, impacting constituents’ perspectives of individuals with records more broadly.

Specifically, social categorization theory articulates the implications and process of how individuals come to assign and distinguish individuals into groups, with much of the theory and evidence pointing to the importance of category salience and the role of group exemplars and prototypes
Additionally, meta-analytic evidence does not empirically support the use of negative campaign advertisements to aid election success [7].

prior evidence on the effects of negative campaign advertisements suggests that they tend to be utilized less by those leading in the polls [4,5] and that Democrats tend to respond more to positive ads, compared to Republicans [6].

In this article, we examine a different possibility. Classical research on political behavior emphasizes that education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge, and participation are central to democratic engagement [17–19]. ... We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.

Online political hostility is positively associated with these indicators, with the strongest associations for political interest, political knowledge, and online participation. These associations are more pronounced for some indicators, especially online and offline participation, among users with more polarized affect directed towards US political leaders. Finally, the results show that engaged but hostile social media users do not simply cater to fringe audiences; they post more frequently and have more friends and followers.

The goal of this study has been to identify correlates of hostile political expression among American X/Twitter users. ... we find that online political hostility is positively associated with several indicators of political engagement and its antecedents.

Combining two years of survey and behavioral data from X/Twitter, we examine associations between online political hostility and indicators of political engagement and its antecedents among American users.

We rely on a data infrastructure combining panel survey data with online behavioral data from X ... The total number of panelists where we were able to link survey responses to their X handle in this period was 2567.

On this basis, we provide three sets of analyses. First, using cross-­sectional and panel analyses, we estimate associations ... Second, we provide suggestive analyses of whether these associations differ by affective polarization ... Third, we examine whether politically hostile users are more active and have greater potential reach

Fig 1 demonstrate positive and statistically significant associations between online political hostility and several indicators of political engagement and its antecedents (consistent with Expectation 1). The associations were obtained after controlling for broad personality traits, income, age, gender, and party identification.

The descriptive pattern suggests that the association between engagement and hostility is often stronger among more affectively polarized users: for those low on affective polarization only four out of eighteen associations, across our three measures of online hostility, are significant, whereas for those high on affective polarization fourteen out of eighteen are significant.
Formal interaction models (Fig 3) show the clearest support for online and offline participation, while the evidence is weaker or inconsistent for more distal antecedents such as education

The count-model results indicate that higher political hostility is associated with more posts and with larger numbers of followers and, to a lesser extent, friends. A change from the mean level of hostility to 1.5 standard deviations above the mean is associated with an increase in the number of posts from around 420 to around 900 and an increase in the number of followers from around 220 to around 370.

In brief, within-person increases in online political engagement are followed by higher levels of online political hostility across the three hostility measures. We also observe some evidence of the reverse temporal association, in which hostility is followed by higher political engagement, although this pattern is weaker and less consistent.
Our evidence does not establish that engagement causes hostility. ... The findings should overall be interpreted as associational rather than causal.

First, the data come from American X/Twitter users. This platform is a public, textbased, and highly political platform, and the associations observed here may not generalize directly to platforms with different affordances, audiences, moderation systems, or norms of interaction.

Finally, while we argue that political engagement is associated with political hostility over and beyond personality, as highlighted in prior research, the utilized Big Five controls do not directly test personality-based accounts centered on more antisocial traits such as Dark Triad traits, sadism, or other antagonistic traits.

Recent research has more strongly emphasized this revisionist view on the costs and benefits of political engagement. Most clearly, the literature on political information processing has argued and found that indicators of political engagement (e.g., partisanship) can be associated with biased assessments of political arguments and news ... Here, we extend and integrate the study of the negative side of political engagement into the study of online politics with a specific focus on online political hostility.

Existing explanations of online hostility can be grouped into at least two distinct literatures. One set of accounts emphasizes socioeconomic marginalization, status threat, and grievance. ... A second set of accounts emphasizes personality and ­emotion-regulation. ... In this article, we examine a different possibility. ... We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.
This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context.

These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.

Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship. However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.

The survey consisted of two primary sections: the first collected demographic information, measures of AI identity, depression, and substance use; the second collected directed friendship nominations.

Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations. Similarly, the positive coefficients for closed triads (transitivity) and negative coefficients for two‑path confirmed that triadic closure... is a fundamental organizing principle within these AI adolescent networks.

Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects... were almost entirely non‑significant across all three schools and substances.

Depression sender and receiver effects were substantively negligible across all schools... and AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.

Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation. Sexual orientation homophily was also significant and positive.

Most notably, School C was the only setting where incoming ties were significantly centralized... indicating a pronounced popularity hierarchy... In contrast, Schools A and B showed no evidence of centralized popularity structures.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time.

Accordingly, the results reported here should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation.

This study addresses this gap by collecting and analyzing first-hand social network data... By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research.

Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties, often through processes of selection... and influence... It remains unclear whether these patterns hold in settings where the student population is predominantly AI.

In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude... By contrast, in our AI-majority sample, substance use showed no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools.
